- Compare directness, endpoint match, conditions, transferability, and uncertainty without counting repeated records independently.

claims.claim: A tocotrienol-rich fraction of palm oil, a lipophilic isoprenoid with a polar chromanol head, is reported to have poor oral bioavailability in humans, supporting low absorption for the structurally related lipophilic isoprenoid CoQ10.
Lycopene, a highly lipophilic C40 isoprenoid, showed only 0.17% systemic appearance after oral intake in humans, illustrating that large lipophilic isoprenoids can have very low oral absorption.

Phytoene, a smaller and more flexible C40 isoprenoid, showed 58.5% absolute bioavailability in humans; this is the strongest high-bioavailability counterexample, but its transferability to the larger, quinone-headed CoQ10 is limited.

content.decision_summary: CoQ10 is a large, highly lipophilic isoprenoid quinone with known poor oral absorption; the closest transferable experimental evidence (tocotrienol, lycopene systemic appearance) supports F < 20%, while the high phytoene value is less transferable.
evidence_gaps: No direct absolute oral bioavailability measurement for CoQ10 is provided in the visible evidence.
The high phytoene and labeled-lycopene absorption values are from compartmental modeling and may not translate to CoQ10 due to differences in molecular size, polarity, and formulation.
Formulation-dependent absorption is a major confounder for lipophilic isoprenoids; the evidence does not specify a CoQ10 formulation.
